prize_parts.citation: For the development of spherical-aberration correction in electron optics, bringing routine atomic-resolution imaging to transmission electron microscopy

statement.case_for: Aberration correction is an invention with a sharp before and after. The Rose hexapole corrector design, the Haider-Urban-Rose realisation of the first working corrector, and Urban's sub-angstrom imaging of materials turned the transmission electron microscope from a diffraction-limited instrument into one that locates individual atoms, light elements, interface defects and point defects as a matter of routine. Two decades of independent confirmation, commercial instruments worldwide and a very wide downstream literature in condensed matter, chemistry and nanoscience make this mature, not premature. The criterion I use, a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, is met in a way that is easy to document: the corrector is a physical object whose authorship is traceable. I put it first because it still seems to me the best fit to the prize criteria on my own list, while stating plainly that I judge it from daily microscopy practice.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are mine to state, since no colleague has yet taken up this candidate. First, it has the narrowest opening support on the shortlist: I am the only member who ranked it at all, so my enthusiasm may reflect field proximity rather than shared judgement. Second, it is an enabling instrument rather than a discovery about nature, and some colleagues may reasonably prefer physics where the result itself is the surprise. Third, attribution is not fully clean. The three credited names omit Ondrej Krivanek, whose STEM corrector work ran in parallel and who, in my general knowledge, shared recent recognition with them, and the boundary between a Physics prize and Chemistry or an instrumentation award is arguable. Against that, competition from the clock and topological candidates is genuine, and I would not insist on B053 if the committee reaches a considered judgement that those are stronger.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the Katori-Ye optical lattice clock first as a clean instrument-level invention: the magic-wavelength lattice, strontium clocks at the 1e-18 level, confirmed by many independent laboratories, with a natural two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of this argument and it is the same test I apply to B053: a concrete invention, independent confirmation, traceable originators. That is why B027 is one of my two alternatives and why I did not leave it low out of any doubt about the physics. My reservation is narrower. The 2005 prize to Hall and Haensch already covers much of the enabling frequency metrology, and Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept, so I would want the citation drawn tightly around the lattice-clock idea and its demonstration. Given that five colleagues placed it first to fourth, it is plainly the safe consensus choice, but being the safe choice is not by itself an argument that it is the best one.

responses.point: Danielsson places topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect second, as a theory-plus-experiment configuration with Kane and Mele supplying the theory and Molenkamp the HgTe realisation, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Hasan and Cava are outside the credit.
responses.response: I share the view that the Kane-Mele idea is original and that the HgTe observation closes the loop, and my own ranking of B057 reflects this. I do qualify one point. The 2016 prize already rewarded topological phases and phase transitions, so the argument for novelty rests on the Z2 classification and the experimental realisation, not on the field in general, and the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang makes the three-name credit less than clean. Danielsson calls it slightly overdue, which I find fair for the physics, but that does not remove the allocation problem, which I regard as more serious here than for B053 or B027. I would support B057 if the committee settles on a credit that withstands that challenge.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit quantum electrodynamics first as the architecture behind most superconducting processors, with theory by Blais and experiments by Wallraff and Schoelkopf, while flagging that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits raises a timing question.
responses.response: The architectural importance is not in doubt, and I accept that the theory-experiment division of credit is natural. My disagreement is about timing and novelty. A prize in 2025 for superconducting circuits makes a 2026 award in the same family look repetitive to many readers, and the strongest case for impact is as a platform for quantum computing, which is still moving fast. I would rather wait than award the area in consecutive years. Johansson knows this field far better than I do, so I treat this as a calibrated reservation about sequencing, not a verdict on the physics.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first as the opening of neutrino astronomy, with Halzen as the scientific driver and Karle as a senior experimental leader, while noting that the collaboration and AMANDA predecessor complicate credit.
responses.response: I find the discovery persuasive and agree that instrument and physics are inseparable, which is the same reason I favour B053. The difficulty I cannot get past is attribution. A detector built and analysed by several hundred people, with AMANDA predecessors and other leading figures, makes a two-name credit hard to defend, and the committee would have to accept that any pairing will be contested. I would take this seriously as a future prize and I rank it below my alternatives for now. If Pearce can show that the principal-originator question is cleaner than I think, I would revisit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards aberration correction as a sufficiently fundamental discovery for the physics prize or as instrumentation better placed elsewhere.
Whether Ondrej Krivanek, not in the supplied credit, should be added or substituted, given the three-person limit; this is from my general knowledge, not the provided files.
Whether the committee can find a defensible three-name credit for topological insulators given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Hasan and Cava.
Whether B027 should win outright on the strength of five members' high rankings, and how much of its recognition overlaps with the 2005 frequency-comb prize.
statement.conflict_note: I am a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers, so spherical-aberration correction (B053) is directly in my professional field. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Rose, Haider or Urban, but I flag the field proximity and would accept recusal from B053 if the committee thinks it appropriate. Also, Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, relevant to his first-ranked circuit QED candidate (B036); I have no specific tie to those candidates beyond the shared institution.
